paragraphs: A person's confidence in a perceptual choice does not necessarily match how often that choice is correct. This makes accuracy alone an incomplete way to explain confidence. The paper introduces a Bayesian framework that treats confidence as something to model within the decision process, rather than simply equating it with observed success.

The framework uses partially observable Markov decision processes, which represent decisions made with incomplete information about the underlying situation. A central contribution is that the model predicts confidence using only information available to the experimenter. This connects a model of the decision maker's uncertainty to observations that can actually be collected in an experiment.

The authors test the framework in two experiments involving judgments about the direction of moving random dots. In both, predicted confidence closely matches the experimental data. The model is also consistent with the hard-easy effect. Together, these findings support the framework as an explanation of confidence in the studied perceptual tasks, while preserving the distinction between confidence and accuracy.
neurips-2015-a-bayesian-framework-for-mo.tldr: A Bayesian model predicts perceptual decision confidence from experimenter-accessible data and closely matches two random-dot motion experiments.

paragraphs: People with the same complex disease can experience very different courses of illness. This paper addresses how to predict an individual's future disease severity while drawing on patterns shared with other patients. It represents a disease trajectory as a continuously valued function of continuous time, so the prediction describes how severity evolves rather than assigning a single disease category.

The proposed hierarchical latent variable model combines information at three resolutions: the whole population, subpopulations, and the individual. Shared patterns provide statistical support for personalized estimates, while individual parameters allow predictions to reflect a particular patient's course. Population and subpopulation parameters are learned offline, and an online procedure dynamically learns the individual-specific parameters.

The authors evaluate the approach by predicting interstitial lung disease progression in patients with scleroderma. They report significant improvements in predictive accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches. This supports the value of combining broad disease patterns with individual adaptation on that task. The stated result concerns forecasting accuracy; improved treatment selection is the motivating clinical possibility.
neurips-2015-a-framework-for-individuali.tldr: A hierarchical model improves personalized disease forecasts by sharing information across population, subpopulation, and individual trajectories.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using the current context while learning which actions pay off. This paper considers discrete contexts with both a time limit and a spending budget. Those constraints link decisions across time: resources used in one context are unavailable for later opportunities, making the exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff more complicated.

The authors first examine equal-cost actions with a known context distribution. When expected rewards are known, their Adaptive Linear Programming method approximates an oracle and achieves near-optimal performance while requiring only the ordering of expected rewards. They then combine this allocation method with upper confidence bounds to learn rewards that are initially unknown.

The resulting UCB-ALP algorithm has logarithmic regret except in certain boundary cases. Regret measures the performance lost relative to the comparison strategy, so this result describes how that loss grows as decisions accumulate. The paper also develops algorithms and similar regret analyses for unknown context distributions or differing costs. Its contribution connects budget allocation with reward learning while retaining the qualifications needed for its logarithmic guarantee.
neurips-2015-algorithms-with-logarithmic.tldr: Adaptive resource allocation combined with upper confidence bounds achieves logarithmic regret for constrained contextual bandits outside certain boundary cases.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether convolutional neural networks operating at the character level can classify text effectively. The input representation makes individual characters the starting point for learning, rather than beginning with word-level representations. The study is empirical: its central question is how well this approach performs when evaluated against established text classification methods.

The authors construct several large-scale datasets and compare character-level networks with a range of alternatives. These include bag-of-words models, n-gram models, and versions using TFIDF weighting. They also compare with word-based convolutional networks and recurrent neural networks. This range of comparisons places the approach alongside both traditional text representations and other neural modeling choices.

The reported findings show that character-level convolutional networks can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results. That establishes characters as a viable starting point for strong text classifiers in the studied settings. The claim is about demonstrated performance across the empirical study, rather than a guarantee that character-level models will always outperform word-based or traditional methods.
neurips-2015-character-level-convolution.tldr: Large-scale experiments show that character-level convolutional networks can achieve competitive or state-of-the-art text classification results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown probability distribution over a discrete population from random samples while protecting the individuals represented in those samples. Its goal combines three requirements: low estimation error, efficient computation, and differential privacy. Accuracy is measured in total variation, which compares the estimated probability distribution with the true one.

The authors propose a general approach for a broad range of structured distribution families. Their estimators are computationally efficient and use nearly the smallest possible number of samples. The theoretical results show that, for many such families, private estimation can come close to the sample requirements and running times of estimation without privacy protection.

Experiments on synthetic mixture models and a large public dataset illustrate the estimators' speed and accuracy. The significance is that distributional structure can make privacy compatible with strong statistical and computational performance. The near-equivalence to non-private estimation is established for the structured families covered by the results, rather than asserted for every possible discrete distribution.
neurips-2015-differentially-private-lear.tldr: For many structured discrete distributions, private estimators nearly match non-private methods in sample requirements and computation.

paragraphs: This paper connects maximum-likelihood estimation for models derived from Luce's choice axiom with the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. The connection includes the Plackett–Luce model. A stationary distribution is a probability distribution that remains unchanged by the chain's transition rule, giving a different mathematical view of the estimation problem.

The authors use this perspective to explain several existing spectral inference algorithms and to develop a new one. For the Plackett–Luce model, the new spectral algorithm is reported to be significantly more accurate than previous spectral approaches. A simple modification also lets it run iteratively, producing estimates that converge to the maximum-likelihood solution.

On a benchmark comprising five datasets, the iterative maximum-likelihood version runs faster than competing approaches. The authors also emphasize that the algorithms are easy to implement. The contribution therefore combines a structural explanation of estimation with practical algorithms: the Markov-chain connection supports both a more accurate spectral estimate and an iterative route to maximum likelihood.
neurips-2015-fast-and-accurate-inference.tldr: A Markov-chain view yields more accurate spectral estimates for Plackett–Luce models and a fast iterative method converging to maximum likelihood.

paragraphs: The paper studies low-rank approximation when a matrix arrives one column at a time and its entries lie between zero and one. Its Streaming Low-rank Approximation algorithm, SLA, aims to recover a compact rank-k representation without keeping the full matrix in memory. Random sparsification reduces work by retaining each entry with a small sampling probability.

The accuracy guarantee is conditional: k times the next singular value must grow more slowly than the square root of the matrix's entry count. Under that condition, SLA's average squared difference from the optimal rank-k approximation approaches zero with high probability as the dimensions grow. This compares two approximations; it does not assert vanishing reconstruction error against every original matrix.

SLA needs one pass for randomly ordered columns and two for arbitrary ordering. Its memory scales as k times the sum of the dimensions, matching the size of its output representation. Runtime is O(δkmn), where δ is the sampling probability. With an appropriate δ and n at least m, it can be as low as O(k log(m)^4 n).
neurips-2015-fast-and-memory-optimal-low.tldr: SLA uses random sparsification to approximate streaming matrices with output-sized memory and conditional asymptotic accuracy.

paragraphs: Natural images contain statistical relationships that can stretch across hundreds of pixels. Modeling an image distribution therefore requires accounting for more than nearby pixel relationships. This paper introduces a recurrent image model designed to capture those extended dependencies using multidimensional long short-term memory units, whose spatial organization suits image data.

The model combines this spatial recurrent structure with two useful properties: it can scale to images of arbitrary size, and its likelihood is computationally tractable. A tractable likelihood makes it possible to evaluate the probability the model assigns to an image. These properties connect the modeling of long-range relationships with a distribution that can be evaluated computationally.

The authors report better quantitative results than the state of the art on several image datasets. They also find promising results for texture synthesis and inpainting, which concern creating textures and filling missing image content. The quantitative comparisons support the model's distributional modeling ability in the evaluated settings, while the application results suggest its usefulness for generating and completing images.
neurips-2015-generative-image-modeling-u.tldr: Spatial LSTMs model long-range image dependencies with tractable likelihoods and improve quantitative results on several image datasets.

paragraphs: When several brain regions are recorded together, researchers may care about both the strength of activity at different frequencies and the phase relationships between channels. This paper develops a Gaussian-process covariance kernel that represents both kinds of information. The motivating problem is inherently multi-output because relationships among recording channels are part of what must be modeled.

The proposed cross-spectral mixture kernel extends the spectral modeling idea beyond a single output. Its role is to describe how multiple observed signals vary together while retaining information about power and phase. This provides a flexible way to express cross-channel frequency relationships within the multi-output Gaussian-process framework, rather than modeling each channel's spectral behavior independently.

To demonstrate the kernel's expressive capacity, the authors place it inside a Bayesian hidden Markov model. Each emission distribution is a multi-output Gaussian process using the new covariance kernel. Results on measured multi-region electrophysiological data illustrate the construction in practice. The stated contribution is a representation of joint spectral relationships and a demonstration on real recordings, rather than a claimed universal performance advantage.
neurips-2015-gp-kernels-for-cross-spectr.tldr: A cross-spectral Gaussian-process kernel models both power and phase relationships across multiple observation channels.

paragraphs: Constituency parsing identifies the grammatical grouping of a sentence. The paper approaches this task with an attention-enhanced sequence-to-sequence model, using a general modeling architecture for a problem traditionally handled by specialized parsers. Its central finding is that this domain-agnostic architecture can achieve strong parsing results under two different training conditions.

When trained on a large synthetic corpus annotated by existing parsers, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the most widely used constituency parsing dataset. With a small human-annotated training set, it matches standard parsers. These are distinct findings: the strongest reported benchmark result uses large-scale parser-generated supervision, while the smaller-data result establishes competitive performance with human annotations.

The authors interpret the small-data performance as evidence of high data efficiency, contrasting it with sequence-to-sequence models without attention. The parser also processes more than one hundred sentences per second in an unoptimized CPU implementation. Together, the findings show that a general sequence architecture can combine parsing accuracy, effective use of limited annotations, and fast processing in the reported setting.
neurips-2015-grammar-as-a-foreign-langua.tldr: An attention-based sequence-to-sequence parser achieves strong accuracy with both large synthetic and small human-annotated training sets.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model collections whose elements tend to be diverse. Their useful mathematical properties do not make likelihood-based parameter learning straightforward. The likelihood involves a kernel L related to the model's kernel K through a potentially intractable spectral decomposition, and its normalizing constant introduces another substantial computational obstacle.

The paper directly parameterizes L, following an existing approach that sacrifices some parameter interpretability. Its main contribution addresses the normalization problem by deriving likelihood bounds for both finite and continuous domains. In the finite case the normalizer involves a large determinant; in the continuous case it involves a Fredholm determinant. The bounds can be evaluated cheaply without approximating the relevant matrix or operator spectrum.

These bounds support inexpensive variational inference and moderately expensive exact Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. The practical significance is a way to perform likelihood-based learning without the spectral calculations that otherwise make it difficult. The method retains the stated interpretability tradeoff of parameterizing L, while opening inference routes for both discrete collections and continuous point-process domains.
neurips-2015-inference-for-determinantal.tldr: Cheap likelihood bounds enable DPP inference on finite and continuous domains without approximating matrix or operator spectra.

paragraphs: Some sequence prediction tasks require following a procedure that counts or remembers earlier parts of a sequence. The paper focuses on simple algorithmically generated sequences with these requirements, using them to examine limitations of standard recurrent networks. The question is whether a learning system can acquire the needed computational behavior directly from sequential examples.

The proposed approach associates a recurrent network with trainable memory. In the stack-augmented setting named by the paper, memory supplies a structured way to grow the model's computational capacity. This targets the ability to count and retain sequences, which the authors identify as necessary for the sequence problems they study.

The authors show that this combination can learn some basic algorithms from sequential data. The result supports a specific route beyond the limitations examined in the paper: allow a network to learn how to use structured memory. Its scope remains the demonstrated basic algorithms and sequence tasks. The contribution is evidence that trainable memory can enable procedural behavior that the standard recurrent approach cannot learn in those settings.
neurips-2015-inferring-algorithmic-patte.tldr: A recurrent network with trainable structured memory learns some basic algorithms from sequences requiring counting and memorization.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to train recurrent neural networks as near-optimal feedback controllers for diverse moving characters. It generates stable, realistic swimming, flying, and walking behaviors across different body shapes, including bipeds and quadrupeds. The method does not require motion capture, task-specific features, or manually specified state machines.

The network combines many feed-forward units, which learn elaborate relationships between states and actions, with a smaller set of recurrent units that maintain memory beyond the physical system's state. Its outputs are velocities. The authors therefore describe it as learning dynamics under an implicit policy, a distinction that clarifies what the network is being trained to represent.

Training alternates supervised learning with trajectory optimization. It also injects noise and includes unexpected changes in task specifications. The trajectory optimizer supplies optimal feedback gains as well as optimal actions, contributing information about responses to deviations. These elements form a training method that supports the reported range of stable behaviors without requiring a separate hand-built control structure for each task.
neurips-2015-interactive-control-of-dive.tldr: Recurrent controllers trained with trajectory optimization generate stable, realistic movement across diverse bodies and tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a structured signal from measurements distorted by a possibly unknown, random nonlinear function. Such distortions can arise in measurement devices or through deliberate quantization, including noisy one-bit measurements. The estimator is regularized Generalized LASSO, which promotes signal structure while treating the observations through a linear measurement model.

With independent standard-normal measurement-matrix entries, earlier results justified recovery up to a scale factor determined by the nonlinearity. This work derives explicit error expressions that become precise as the signal and measurement dimensions grow. Its main result equates the estimator's asymptotic performance to that under an effective linear model with a rescaled signal and additive noise.

The effective scale and noise variance are determined by expectations involving the nonlinear link applied to a standard-normal variable. Thus, the equivalence concerns estimation performance under the stated asymptotic setting, not literal equality of the measurement mechanisms. A consequence is that the Lloyd–Max quantizer minimizes the LASSO estimation error in the quantizer-design problem considered by the result.
neurips-2015-lasso-with-non-linear-measu.tldr: Under Gaussian measurements, Generalized LASSO has asymptotically equivalent error for nonlinear observations and a corresponding noisy linear model.

paragraphs: A detailed model may describe individual behavior well, while a coarser model captures population-wide behavior more naturally. This paper asks how to integrate those models when both are conveniently expressed using latent variables. The challenge is to connect their descriptions without reducing their relationship solely to agreement between selected expectations.

The proposed method, latent Bayesian melding, is motivated by combining the distributions that the two models imply over population statistics. It uses a logarithmic opinion pool framework for this combination. This shifts the focus from generalized moment matching, which aligns expectations, toward pooling distributions associated with the individual-level and population-level descriptions.

The authors study electricity disaggregation, a single-channel blind source separation problem, as a practical case. They report significantly more accurate predictions than an approach based only on generalized moment matching. This result supports the benefit of the proposed integration in that case study. The broader methodological contribution is a way to bring population information into detailed individual models when latent variables are useful at both levels.
neurips-2015-latent-bayesian-melding-for.tldr: Latent Bayesian melding combines individual and population models through distribution pooling and improves predictions in an electricity disaggregation case study.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves selecting dependency relationships among variables. As the number of variables grows, the possible structures create a difficult search problem. This paper presents a method for datasets containing thousands of variables without requiring structure constraints, addressing both the search for local relationships and the optimization of the overall network.

The first component explores candidate parent sets for each node. It uses an approximate score that can be computed in constant time to direct attention toward promising candidates. The second component improves an existing ordering-based structure optimization algorithm. The authors prove that this revised algorithm achieves a higher score than its original formulation.

Experiments on very large datasets, reaching ten thousand nodes, show consistent improvements over the state of the art. The two components address complementary parts of the scaling problem: efficiently identifying plausible local choices and improving the structure search that uses them. The formal result concerns the optimization score, while the empirical comparisons establish the method's reported advantage on the evaluated large datasets.
neurips-2015-learning-bayesian-networks-.tldr: Efficient parent-set exploration and improved structure optimization scale Bayesian-network learning to datasets with up to ten thousand nodes.

paragraphs: This paper improves stochastic optimization by changing how training terms are sampled. It targets linearly convergent methods, including Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient and Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent. The key idea is to use data-dependent information about how smoothly loss functions behave near the optimum when choosing which terms to process.

The authors develop non-uniform sampling strategies for a large family of penalized empirical risk minimization problems. These strategies exploit local smoothness while maintaining convergence guarantees. Their theoretical bounds quantify the advantage available from that local information, establishing provable acceleration that can be significant for some problems.

Numerical experiments support the theory. The paper also presents more aggressive ways to exploit local smoothness, which perform even better in practice. These are complementary claims: the guaranteed methods supply a formal account of why local smoothness can help, while the more aggressive methods demonstrate additional empirical gains. The contribution is to make the behavior of losses near the solution useful in the sampling decisions that drive optimization.
neurips-2015-local-smoothness-in-varianc.tldr: Sampling strategies based on local loss smoothness provably accelerate variance-reduced optimization and show supporting empirical gains.

paragraphs: Market scoring rules aggregate probabilistic beliefs in algorithmic prediction markets. Their familiar incentive properties assume myopic, risk-neutral participants. This paper examines how market prices incorporate private beliefs when participants are risk-averse, asking what their trades reveal once willingness to take risk affects the decision.

Under mild regularity conditions, the authors show that a myopic risk-averse trader reveals a risk-neutral probability conditional on the latest market state, rather than the trader's true subjective probability. Consequently, the market scoring rule behaves like an opinion pool for participants' underlying beliefs. The current market state matters to the probability that trading elicits.

The form of pooling depends on utility. The logarithmic market scoring rule acts as a logarithmic pool for constant absolute risk aversion, and as a linear pool for the specified atypical budget-constrained utility with decreasing absolute risk aversion. The authors also interpret the market maker as a Bayesian learner under these conditions, even with static beliefs. These results describe precisely qualified aggregation behavior rather than unrestricted truthful revelation.
neurips-2015-market-scoring-rules-act-as.tldr: Under specified conditions, market scoring rules pool risk-averse traders' beliefs instead of directly eliciting their subjective probabilities.

paragraphs: Natural Neural Networks aim to speed training by adapting a network's internal representation. The target is the conditioning of the Fisher matrix, which describes a geometry relevant to parameter updates. Improving that conditioning makes the parameterization more suitable for optimization, so the method changes how learning is organized within the network.

The paper gives a concrete construction that reparameterizes weights to implicitly whiten the representation at each layer. This transformation preserves the network's feed-forward computation. The proposed Projected Natural Gradient Descent algorithm, PRONG, trains these networks while spreading the cost of reparameterization across many parameter updates, making the additional transformations more affordable.

The authors connect PRONG closely to the Mirror Descent online learning algorithm. They demonstrate benefits on supervised and unsupervised tasks and illustrate scalability by training on the ImageNet Challenge dataset. The contribution combines a representation-based approach to improving optimization geometry with a training procedure designed to manage its cost. The reported applications support its practical use across the learning settings examined.
neurips-2015-natural-neural-networks-a45.tldr: Natural Neural Networks accelerate training through internal reparameterization, with PRONG amortizing the cost across many updates.

paragraphs: Some sequence problems require outputs that identify positions in the input. Their available output choices therefore change with input length, creating a difficulty for models with a fixed output dictionary. Pointer Networks address this by learning output sequences whose discrete elements refer directly to members of the input sequence.

The architecture repurposes neural attention. Instead of using attention only to combine encoder representations into a context vector, it uses attention to select an input position as the output. This makes the available choices automatically follow the input's size and provides a neural mechanism for problems such as variable-length sorting and combinatorial optimization.

Using training examples alone, the authors learn approximate solutions for planar convex hulls, Delaunay triangulations, and the planar Travelling Salesman Problem. The models improve over sequence-to-sequence models with input attention and generalize beyond the maximum training lengths in the reported experiments. These findings support learning discrete geometric procedures with variable output dictionaries, while the optimization solutions remain approximate.
neurips-2015-pointer-networks-2e49ca77e2.tldr: Pointer Networks use attention to select input positions, learning approximate geometric solutions with output choices that vary with input length.

paragraphs: The paper develops locality-sensitive hashing for approximate near-neighbor search using angular distance. This type of hashing organizes points so that similar ones can be found efficiently. The authors establish an LSH family whose resulting search algorithm achieves the asymptotically optimal running-time exponent, addressing a central theoretical measure of search efficiency.

The method also improves on hyperplane LSH in practice, connecting the theoretical exponent with an implementable algorithm. The authors introduce a multiprobe version and evaluate the approach on both real and synthetic datasets. These experiments complement the asymptotic result by examining practical performance, which the abstract distinguishes from earlier algorithms with the same optimal-exponent property.

A further contribution is a fine-grained lower bound on the quality of angular-distance LSH families. It shows that the proposed family's tradeoff between evaluation time and quality is close to optimal within a natural class of hashing functions. This qualifies the optimality claim: the exponent is asymptotically optimal, while the evaluation-cost tradeoff is near-optimal for the specified class.
neurips-2015-practical-and-optimal-lsh-f.tldr: An angular-distance hashing method combines an asymptotically optimal search exponent with practical improvements over hyperplane LSH.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement-learning tasks run for a fixed or bounded period, making episodic finite-horizon models a natural fit. This paper studies how many episodes are required to guarantee a desired level of performance with high probability. That sample-complexity question concerns the amount of interaction needed for reliable learning, rather than only the quality of a learned policy.

The authors derive upper and lower probably approximately correct bounds. Ignoring logarithmic terms, the upper bound scales with the square of the state count, the action count, the square of the horizon, and inverse squared accuracy. The lower bound has the same horizon, action, and accuracy dependence, but only linear dependence on the state count.

The bounds therefore agree up to logarithmic factors and one additional factor in the number of states. The upper-bound analysis uses Bernstein's inequality to improve horizon dependence from at least cubic in earlier bounds to quadratic. The paper also supplies the first lower bound of its kind for this setting, clarifying both achievable episode requirements and a remaining gap.
neurips-2015-sample-complexity-of-episod.tldr: New episodic reinforcement-learning bounds achieve quadratic horizon dependence and match apart from logarithmic terms and a state-count factor.

paragraphs: A nonparametric hidden Markov model must learn both temporal structure and an appropriate number of hidden states. Common approaches fix a truncation or make only small local changes to the state space. This paper develops inference for the sticky hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model that adapts the state count while processing only a few sequences at a time.

A new variational bound penalizes redundant or irrelevant states, allowing optimization to favor a useful state space. Birth proposals use observed data statistics to introduce states that can escape local optima. Merge and delete proposals remove ineffective states, simplifying the model and reducing the cost of subsequent computation.

Experiments cover speaker diarization, motion capture, and epigenetic chromatin data. The resulting models are more compact, more interpretable, and better aligned with ground-truth segmentations than competitors. The released Python implementation can parallelize local inference across sequences. Together, the results show how actively revising model complexity can support both scalable inference and clearer temporal structure in the evaluated applications.
neurips-2015-scalable-adaptation-of-stat.tldr: Scalable variational inference adds, merges, and deletes hidden states to learn more compact and interpretable temporal models.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse principal components that use disjoint sets of input variables and jointly capture as much variance as possible. Computing one component at a time and then deflating the data is a greedy approach that can be suboptimal. The authors instead optimize multiple components together, explicitly accounting for how their variable choices interact.

Their combinatorial algorithm constructs the components by solving multiple maximum-weight bipartite matching problems. It guarantees captured variance within a multiplicative factor arbitrarily close to one of the optimum. This provides a near-optimality statement for the specified problem of multiple sparse components with disjoint supports, rather than for every formulation of sparse PCA.

The computational cost grows as a low-degree polynomial in input dimension but exponentially in rank. That rank dependence is a substantial condition on practical use; the authors note that the algorithm can operate effectively on a low-dimensional sketch. Experiments on real datasets show that it outperforms deflation-based approaches in many cases, supporting the value of jointly selecting components.
neurips-2015-sparse-pca-via-bipartite-ma.tldr: Bipartite matchings jointly optimize disjoint sparse principal components with near-optimal variance capture, at a cost exponential in rank.

paragraphs: Activity across a population of neurons varies in several ways. The paper distinguishes single-neuron randomness, short-timescale neural dynamics, and slower changes in firing properties. Those slower changes, called non-stationarity, motivate a model that can describe both ongoing population dynamics and changes in firing rates between experimental trials.

The authors introduce a hierarchical dynamics model to represent these sources of temporal structure together. Its hierarchy allows inter-trial firing-rate modulation to coexist with neural population dynamics. They also derive a Bayesian Laplace propagation algorithm for fast posterior inference, providing a computational procedure for estimating the model from observed activity.

Applied to population recordings from primary visual cortex, the model gives a better account of neural firing structure than existing stationary dynamics models. This supports including between-trial modulation when explaining the recordings studied. The broader significance is methodological: a model that allows firing properties to change can characterize shared neural variability more faithfully than one whose dynamics assume stationarity in this setting.
neurips-2015-unlocking-neural-population.tldr: A hierarchical dynamics model captures between-trial firing changes and better explains visual-cortex recordings than stationary dynamics models.
